source.title: Scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data
source.authors: A. Jain; Andrea Montanari; Eren Sasoglu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some mathematical notation is garbled by text extraction, but the relevant empirical results and conclusions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling-law behavior for weighted mixtures of original and surrogate data, and qualifies it by reporting that fitted exponents can differ between data sources and that the proposed law is an empirical approximation. It does not test language-model size/token/compute scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling-law fits and compares the predicted test-loss curves with experiments. Its references to language-model scaling laws are background, not results from this study. The fitted exponents and mixture-curve comparisons below bear on V5 and V7; parameter-count, compute-budget, and downstream-task claims are not tested.
record.test_reason: Its own experiments fit test-error-versus-sample-count power laws (A + B·n^-β) for small neural nets and a CIFAR10 ResNet. It also checks a power-law mixture law (Eq. 4) against measured test error. That makes it a new-setting (image/classification, mixed-data training) result on V5's data-scaling form, though weak. All fits are data-only, over about 1.5–2 orders of magnitude, with fit quality shown only in figures. Most rows are classical statistical models (logistic, ridge, Cox-lasso), not the kind of system the versions name.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also stress two headline findings. First, surrogate data reduce test error even when unrelated to the original data, which they trace to Stein's paradox. Second, optimally weighted ERM is crucial, and unweighted mixing can degrade with more surrogate data. They present Eq. (4) as an empirical approximation that can pick α and the amount of surrogate data, which may fail if real and surrogate exponents differ substantially.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a weighted-ERM scaling law for test error versus original/surrogate sample counts and mixture weight. It does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments over parameters, training tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents vary across datasets and model settings. For high-dimensional ridge regression, the reported exponent changes from 1.57 with fixed λ = 2⁻¹⁰ to 0.94 when λ is selected by validation. The paper also reports that real-data and surrogate-data exponents can differ.

fits_no_version.finding: In classical statistical models (logistic, ridge, Cox-lasso), test error vs sample count is fitted by a power law with offset. The fitted exponent depends on regularization procedure: ridge β=1.57 with fixed λ=2^-10 vs 0.94 with validated λ. Theory gives β=1 asymptotically, but moderate-sample curves fit other β.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-size scaling exponents in classical estimators depend on regularization tuning and finite-sample regime.

fits_no_version.finding: A mixture scaling law (Eq. 4) predicts test error as a function of original count n, surrogate count m and weight α in classical models. The authors note it only approximates the exact high-dimensional asymptotics for ridge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test error on weighted real/surrogate mixtures follows a composite power-law form in n, m and α.

record.problems: The empirical models and datasets are limited to the reported settings and do not test language-model pretraining or compute-optimal allocation. Many mixture-curve comparisons are presented as plots without numerical error summaries or uncertainty intervals. The authors describe the law as an approximation and note that differing real/surrogate exponents could make it inaccurate.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant reported scaling outcomes were intentionally omitted. Additional plotted combinations of n and m are shown separately in Figures 7, 9, 13, 15, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, and 30; the retained curve-comparison rows summarize the paper's stated findings for those figure sets.

untested.parts: All of it: LM pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: extrapolation over orders of magnitude.
All of it: architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Parameter and compute scaling; ranges beyond ~2 orders of magnitude in data; video; repeated data; fine-tuning; large models. Only sample-count scaling of small nets and a small ResNet is tested.
All of it: downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Untested for neural/LM-type systems. No neural-net row compares fitting or setup choices. The βor≠βsu remark is stated without numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V7 'supports' label is dropped. Exponents differing across unrelated datasets and models is not V7's claim. The one fitting-choice effect (ridge λ procedure) is in a classical model, so it goes under fits_no_version. Its V5 label is narrowed to neural-net rows. The V5 support is weak: data-only scaling, short ranges, figure-only fit quality.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating from small language-model runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling-law behavior for sample counts and mixtures of real and surrogate data in statistical models, classification, NLP features, images, and survival analysis. It does not test language-model pretraining, video, repeated training data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predicting downstream-task performance from language-model scale or pretraining loss.

The study reports setup-dependent fitted sample-scaling exponents and warns the proposed law may be inaccurate if real- and surrogate-data exponents differ substantially. It does not test parameter-counting choices, language-model training schedules, compute-optimal allocation, or published-law disagreements directly.

relationships.condition: Data-only scaling of small neural nets and a 9-layer CIFAR10 ResNet, including weighted real/surrogate mixtures, over ~1.5–2 orders of magnitude in samples
relationships.reason: Power-law-plus-offset fits track test error vs n and m (R2, R6, R7). Eq. (4), built from these power laws, matches mixture test error across n, m and α in the figures (R14, R15, R16). Evidence is figure-only, with no fit statistics.
relationships.display_finding: Power laws with offsets tracked test error against real and surrogate sample sizes, and their combined expression matched mixture errors across sample sizes and mixture weights, without reported fit statistics.
